intuition: Process meetings by their start times. Keep the end times of meetings still in progress in a min-heap. Before adding a meeting, remove every meeting that has ended. The largest number of simultaneous meetings is the number of rooms required.

A min-heap exposes the earliest active end. Before adding a new meeting, remove every end at or before its start; those rooms have become available. The remaining entries describe meetings competing with the new one for space at that instant.

The room requirement is the largest active count, not the active count after the final start. That peak is necessary because all those meetings overlap simultaneously, and sufficient because ended rooms can always be reused. Equal end and start times do not overlap in this scheduling problem.

steps: For [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]], start sorting leaves the input order unchanged. Begin with active_ends=[] and peak=0.
At start 0, no room can be freed. Push end 30, giving heap [30] and peak=1.
At start 5, earliest end 30 is still in the future. Push 10, yielding [10,30] and peak=2.
At start 15, pop end 10 because its meeting has ended. End 30 remains active.
Push end 20; the heap is [20,30]. Two meetings are again active, so peak remains 2.
Return peak=2. One room hosts the long meeting, and the other is reused for [5,10] then [15,20].

codeNotes.note: Remove every completed meeting, including one ending exactly at start, so heap size represents current occupancy accurately.
Store end times rather than full meetings because future reuse decisions depend only on when active rooms become free.
An earlier busy moment may require more rooms than the final heap size. Retaining the maximum preserves that capacity requirement.

keyDecision: Remove end times <= the new start time before counting active meetings.

concept.question: How does the busiest moment determine the number of rooms?
intuition: A total meeting count ignores room reuse. What matters is how many meetings are active simultaneously.

Process starts chronologically and keep active meeting ends in a minimum-priority queue. Before a new meeting begins, release every meeting whose end has arrived. Add the new end and remember the greatest active count.
concept.observation: Release all ends at or before the next start; equal endpoints can reuse a room.
approach: Remove ended meetings from the active-end queue.
Add the new meeting and remember the peak active count.
concept.correctness: At each start, removing ended meetings leaves exactly those overlapping the new meeting. Their count plus the new one is the simultaneous demand. No schedule can use fewer than the peak demand. Reusing released rooms realizes that demand without extra rooms, so the maximum active count is sufficient and necessary.

complexity.explanation: Sorting and priority-queue updates take linear-times-logarithmic work. The active ends can occupy linear memory.
